title: World Models Have to Learn What to Ignore Before They Can Plan
dek: Recent work on robot and driving world models keeps arriving at one move: split what the action changes from the colour, the camera and the physics you cannot see.
by: Draft for team review · written by Claude Code from published research and engineering writing · checked in code
lead: What is a world model in AI? A learned simulator that predicts what an action will do. It plans well once its state keeps action consequences, drops appearance and viewpoint, and infers hidden physics.

cover.alt: Faded cards show a T-shaped block in many colours; in front, a crisp T outline with a push arrow and its predicted pose.
cover.caption: A world model keeps the block's pose and the push, and lets its colour and texture fall away.

description: What is a world model in AI? A learned simulator that predicts what an action does. New work shows it plans well only when it learns what to ignore.
keywords: what is a world model in AI
decisions: Add an action-prediction loss when observations vary in appearance
Give hidden physics its own latent and fit it at test time
Keep camera motion out of the scene state
Gather interaction data with a play policy before collecting task demos

items.meaning: A learned simulator that predicts the next state of a scene from the current state and an action.
A compact vector an encoder computes from observations, standing in for the scene during prediction and planning.
A model that reads the states before and after a step and predicts the action taken between them.
A learnable vector that captures hidden conditions such as friction or mass and conditions every prediction the world model makes.
A scene representation that stays the same when only the camera moves.
Planning by scoring candidate action sequences inside a model, executing the first step, then planning again.
Training a policy to imitate demonstrated actions with ordinary supervised learning.

body.text: A world model predicts what your action will do next

body: A world model is a learned simulator: give it the current state and an action, and it predicts the next state. Robots plan with it by imagining moves before making them. Here's why it matters right now. On Push-T, where a robot pushes a T-shaped block into place, one training change lifted planning success «from 9.1% to 77.2%». The planner didn't change.

Let's pin the vocabulary down. The state is everything the model tracks about the scene. Usually it's a latent state, a compact vector an encoder computes from camera images. Action-conditioned dynamics is the learned rule `z_next = f(z, a)`: latent now plus action in, latent next out. Planning searches over action sequences, rolls each through `f`, and keeps the one that ends nearest the goal.

That loop hides a trap, and it runs through everything below. The encoder sees pixels, and pixels carry plenty that has nothing to do with control: colour, texture, lighting, where the camera stands. A model can predict the next frame beautifully and still blur what the action did. We'll follow the pushed block through recent arXiv work that attacks the problem piece by piece.

body.text: Appearance can hide the one thing a planner needs

body: Start with the T-block, now rendered in 24 different looks. A new arXiv paper on intrinsic dynamics names what's at stake: «the relationship between actions and their consequences». The worry is that «visual variations unrelated to the underlying control process can obscure this relationship in learned representations». Change the block's colour often enough and the encoder may spend its effort on colour.

body.alt: Two frames pass through a shared encoder into latents that are concatenated so an inverse model predicts the action.
body.caption: Concat IDM asks the latents to explain the action, and that loss flows back into the shared encoder.

body: forward prediction can still be exact on those transitions

We retraced their argument, and it's neat. Action predictability is «the ability to reconstruct an action from consecutive latent states». An inverse dynamics model, or IDM, does that reconstruction. It reads the state before and after a step and guesses the action between them. If the encoder merges different outcomes of different actions, no IDM can tell them apart. So inverse error can't fall to zero.

The surprise is the other half of the result. On those same merged transitions, «forward prediction can still be exact». Read that twice. A forward model, the kind that predicts the next state, can look perfect on its own loss after throwing away the distinction a planner needs. Its training curve gives you no warning.

Their fix, Concat IDM, «predicts actions from concatenated latent states and updates the shared encoder using action labels already available in offline trajectories». No new data, no planner change. Over «three independent training runs on Push-T with 24 appearances», success rose from 9.1% to 77.2%. The gain was 52.9 percentage points larger than with a single appearance. We think that's the telling part: the fix pays most where appearance varies most.

body.text: Hidden physics belongs in a latent you fit at test time

body: Appearance is noise you want to discard. Friction is the opposite: it matters, and you can't see it. A new arXiv paper on T2-Z frames the problem as factors «neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules». Push our T-block on a waxed table, then on rubber. Same pixels, different slide.

body.alt: Two training stages alternate between learning the world model and fitting latents, then test time fits a new latent.
body.caption: T2-Z alternates what is frozen during training, then fits only a fresh environment latent at test time.

body: T2-Z adds an environment latent, a small learnable vector that conditions every prediction. Training alternates. One stage «fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments». The other «freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents». Nothing labels the friction. Latent structure is left «to emerge purely through world prediction», so the vector becomes whatever the model needed to predict well.

Test time is the clever part. The world model stays frozen, and a fresh latent is optimized from «one or more test-time interactions». Picture the robot nudging the block, watching it slide, and adjusting the latent until predictions match. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world tasks, object prediction error fell from 15.20 to 7.00. Action success rose from 33.73% to 72.96%.

One property deserves a highlight. T2-Z «can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory». We agree this is the most useful property for builders. A world model that adapts from one push, with no retraining, is far easier to carry into a room it has never seen.

body.text: The camera is not part of the world

body: Driving scenes bring a third nuisance: viewpoint. A new arXiv paper on GeoState notes that recent 3D world models «increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states». GFMs are large pretrained networks that infer depth and shape from images. The catch is that «the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation». Move the camera and the state shifts, though the world stood still.

body.alt: Cameras around one scene-state block cast rays into it, while camera motion runs on a separate track below.
body.caption: GeoState predicts the scene state on its own and models camera motion as a separate stream.

body: GeoState's answer is architectural. In its design, «a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state». A geometry decoder reads that state back by casting camera rays into it. The world model predicts how the scene state evolves, and «camera motion is modeled separately». Two streams, then: what the world does, and where you're looking from.

The payoff is flexibility. Predicted states «can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras». The model also keeps «a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment». GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo and «generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes». For our T-block the lesson matches the one about colour. Keep the observer out of the state.

body.text: A robot at play can gather its own training data

body: Every model above needs interaction data, and robot hours are expensive. A new arXiv paper on DSP, short for Dexterity from Supervised Play, attacks the supply problem. The robot learns «a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning», then runs it on its own «to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model». Minutes in, hours out.

Behavior cloning means imitating demonstrated actions with supervised learning. The play policy isn't trying to finish a task. It's trying to touch things in varied ways, which is exactly what a world model needs to see. Contact-rich manipulation, such as a multifingered hand reorienting an object in its grip, is where that variety matters most.

The same play policy then helps plan. Under model-predictive control, or MPC, the robot proposes action sequences, scores each inside the world model, executes the first step and replans. DSP uses the play policy for «proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model». Finally, a faster goal-conditioned policy is distilled «through self-play within the learned world model».

The real-world results are striking. DSP «outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate». It also «achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490 times less interaction data». We'd read the second figure with care, since it compares against RL on this task setup only. Still, a world model that turns minutes of play into a planner is a strong argument.

body.caption: The DSP loop turns minutes of human play into a world model and a planner.

body.text: The common move is separating control from nuisance

body: Step back and the shared idea is plain. Each method splits the state into what the action changes and what merely varies. Concat IDM forces the latent to keep action consequences under changing looks. T2-Z moves hidden physics into its own vector. GeoState moves the camera out of the scene state. DSP supplies varied contact so the split has something to learn from.

In our view, this is the working definition of a good world model. Predicting pixels isn't the job. Predicting the consequences of actions, under the conditions that change those consequences, is the job. The intrinsic-dynamics result shows the distinction is practical: a forward model can be exact on merged transitions and still useless to a planner.

They part ways on supervision. Concat IDM leans on «action labels already available in offline trajectories». T2-Z learns its latent «without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take». DSP needs no task-specific demonstrations, only minutes of human play. GeoState borrows rich geometric priors from pretrained models. Each choice moves the cost somewhere else.

Representation splits them too. Concat IDM and T2-Z plan in a learned latent space. GeoState keeps an explicit geometry state you can decode under any camera. DSP's world model serves both a planner and a distilled policy. Explicit geometry is easier to inspect. Latents are cheaper to plan in. None of this work measures that trade on a shared task.

body.text: Composing the pieces is the open problem

body: Here's what remains unsettled. Each result fixes one nuisance on its own testbed: appearance on Push-T, physics across simulated and real tasks, viewpoint on driving scenes, data supply on dexterous manipulation. We haven't seen them stacked. Does a view-decoupled state still need an action-predictability loss? Does a test-time latent survive when the camera moves too?

Scale is the second gap. Push-T with 24 appearances is a controlled test, and the authors say as much by calling their work «controlled appearance-diversity comparisons». Real kitchens vary in ways nobody enumerates. Long-horizon planning is also thin. That's where small prediction errors compound over many imagined steps, and where world models tend to crack.

What would settle it? One robot and one world model, trained on play data, with a view-decoupled state, an action-predictive encoder and a test-time environment latent. Then evaluate on unseen looks, unseen physics and unseen cameras together, against each piece alone. If the gains add up, world models have a recipe. If they don't, we'll learn which nuisance matters most.
What is a world model in AI?

A world model is a learned simulator that predicts what happens next when an agent takes an action. Robots use one to plan by imagining moves before making them. Recent work suggests it plans well only when its state keeps the consequences of actions and drops nuisance such as appearance and camera viewpoint.
How do robots use world models for planning?

Mostly through model-predictive control: propose action sequences, score them inside the world model, execute the first step, then replan. DSP uses a play policy learned from human play for «proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model». In real-world tests that design «outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate».
Can a world model adapt to a new environment without retraining?

Yes, if it carries a latent you can fit at test time. T2-Z keeps the world model frozen and optimizes a fresh environment latent from interaction. It «can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory». That lets one model cope with friction, mass and rule changes nobody told it about.
